item.title: Why Discussing Ariana Grande's Weight Helps No One
item.description:
Body Image

Why Discussing Ariana Grande's Weight Helps No One

Talking about Ariana Grande's weight doesn’t help you or your daughter. Do this instead.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Ariana Grande’s physical appearance has become a popular topic of discussion on social and mainstream media.
  • Focusing on celebrities’ bodies discourages personal agency in promoting our own healthy body image.
  • We can best help our daughters by modeling full lives that are not centered on celebrity culture.
  • Eating disorders require professional attention and cannot be resolved with dialogue on social media.
Source: Pexels/Andrea Piacquadio

The internet has exploded with discussion and debate about Ariana Grande’s physical appearance, which has been described by many as sickly and emaciated. Whether on Instagram, Threads, Facebook, or even in mainstream news outlets, everyone has an opinion about the superstar’s health status and its possible effects on girls’ and women’s body image. These reactions are part of a larger dialogue about the disturbing resurgence of an extreme thin ideal in celebrity and influencer culture.

Those who endorse the need to publicly “call out” Grande’s physical appearance correctly argue that discussion of unrealistic body ideals is important. We know from scientific research that the thin ideal is a major source of body dissatisfaction and negative body image (Paterna et al., 2021), and that pursuing it is associated with eating disorders and disordered eating (Thompson & Stice 2001).

But the focus on Grande specifically—or indeed on any celebrity—is not the best use of our energy if we truly seek to promote healthy body image for ourselves, our daughters, and even for the celebrity herself.

Why it doesn’t help you. Although it may feel like you are accomplishing something by posting or commenting on images of Ariana Grande, these are reactions rather than actions directed to improving your own body image. Humans thrive when their behavior is independent and self-directed (Ryan et al., 2021). Instead of adding to the thousands of comments reiterating the same points, ask yourself whether you are too involved in these posts, and if so, why. It may be uncomfortable to acknowledge that excessive talk about bodies takes up a substantial amount of our time and while this may not be our fault—media and diet culture bombard women with body-focused content—it is our opportunity to recognize it and opt out.

  • Consider instead: Slowly start to unfollow accounts that only focus on bodies, particularly celebrity bodies, and begin to replace them with those focused on a skill, hobby, or talent that you would like to cultivate. Meditation? Learning a new language? Crafting? Gardening? Opportunities abound.

Why it doesn’t help your daughter. Although some have argued that we must talk to our daughters about Grande and other extremely thin celebrities as a preventive measure, consider that research shows moms are the most prominent influencers in their daughters’ body image development (see Boseovski & Gallagher, 2024). If you are preoccupied with celebrity culture, you are sending her the message that it is an important way to spend her time.

  • Consider instead: Model for your daughter that your life is rich with purpose in your world to encourage her to follow suit. Discuss with her that the world of celebrities does not represent our lives and that celebrities’ pressures result in extreme behaviors. To be sure, it can be fun occasionally to visit this other world and enjoy the fashion and entertainment that comes with it, but it is necessary to establish clear boundaries.

Why it doesn’t help Ariana Grande. Many people feel that they “know” celebrities and that they have insight into their personal lives. But these are only parasocial relationships. We do not know Ariana Grande or the particulars of her experience. And if she is indeed living with an eating disorder, it is important to recognize that professional help is necessary, and that we are not in a position to make casual diagnoses. Anorexia Nervosa has one of the highest rates of mortality among psychiatric disorders (Lai et al., 2025) and it cannot be treated on social media. Implying anything otherwise might also discourage girls and women from seeking professional guidance for their own disordered eating.

Let’s regroup, exercise our personal agency, and move on to legitimate ways of working toward a healthy body image.

item.title: What We Lose When We Focus on Speaking Skills
item.description:
Education

What We Lose When We Focus on Speaking Skills

We spend years learning to speak. But how many of us really learn to listen?

Posted August 13, 2026

Source: Shchus/Shutterstock

Think back to the hours you spent learning to speak.

Speech therapy in elementary school, if you needed it. Book reports at the front of the room. Debate team for some of us. The public-speaking unit in tenth-grade English. PowerPoint slide decks in college and every year after that into the workplace. Somewhere in there, you probably picked up a book or read a blog on public speaking — they never leave the bestseller lists. Think about the culture’s worship of the TED Talk, the Moth story hour, or other examples of “The Sage on the Stage.”

Now consider the hours you spent learning to listen. For most of us, it’s about zero. A few of us got lucky — therapists, some coaches, a few others. Maybe you read an emotional intelligence book or sat through a corporate workshop on active listening where you practiced nodding and smiling.

And notice what that workshop actually taught you. Maintain eye contact. Orient your body toward the speaker. Mirror their posture. Reflect back what you heard: So what I’m hearing is… These are great instructions for looking like a good listener. Which raises the obvious question nobody in the workshop asks: why learn to look like you are paying attention when you know actual attention isn’t about performing?

Listening turns out to be one of the better predictors of how things go for people — in relationships, in leadership, in negotiations, in performance. In many studies, it outperforms personality, technical skills, even IQ.

Meanwhile, we’re doing less of it all the time. We are not just bad at listening, but getting worse, in a time when we need to listen to each other more than ever.

The consequences are real—from personal relationships to politics, and you already know what they feel like from the other side. Think of the last time you tried to tell a story to someone who wasn’t fully there. Eyes flicking to the phone, scanning over your shoulder, then the door. Nodding too early, yessing too fast. A hollow echo back of your words to prove they were doing… something.

And what happened to you? Maybe you fumbled through, or you sped up. You cut out the part that was actually the point — the embarrassing part, the funny part, the part that drove home the emotion. You wrapped it up early or told yourself the story wasn’t that interesting anyway. But maybe it wasn’t entirely your fault, maybe the listener just didn’t help you along.

I watched this in my office for years before I understood what I was seeing.

A couple comes in. One partner has clearly done their homework on active listening. They turn toward their spouse, smile and nod, drop in the mm-hmms at the right places. They reflect back something like So what I’m hearing is that you felt alone at your sister’s wedding. From a distance, they get passing marks for their acting.

But the other half of the couple says it all with their body language, folded arms and flat, if not skeptical face.

What was missing wasn’t skill, but genuine curiosity — the real kind, the kind that wants to know something it doesn’t already know. We can all feel the difference between being attentive and acting attentively, on either side.

The partner who doesn’t feel heard doesn’t open up further. The quality of your listening is what tells the other person whether it’s safe to keep taking those risks — and those risks and vulnerability are where the magic happen, whether you’re in a marriage, a negotiation, or a meeting where everyone is staring at their feet wondering who else will speak up.

So don’t listen just to respond, listen to regulate. Not to control or manipulate the other person, but to steady them to safely open up, internally and externally. When they feel heard, they get calmer in their minds and bodies, and a calmer person gets clearer, more honest, more creative, and more willing to take a risk. You are, in a real physiological sense, co-regulating them into the best conditions for them to problem-solve and collaborate.

Good listening is not a nice thing to do for friends and family, nor is it an important thing to do for colleagues and clients. It’s the most powerful tool we have in communication, and it costs you nothing but the effort of trying to get curious. Heck, I spent an hour last week listening to someone explain the nuances of the global gravel industry to me. I could have been bored, but instead I let myself get genuinely interested in some of the threads of the conversation, and had a great time.

You have to get curious — actually, authentically curious — about the specific person in front of you. As Kate Murphy puts it in her book on listening: You don’t need to act like you’re paying attention if you are, in fact, paying attention. I'll add to that: You don't need to look curious if you are, in fact, authentically curious.

The last thing you need to know:

  • We spend our lives learning to speak, but almost never to listen, and it shows.
  • Listening skills predict success across the board.
  • Don’t just listen to respond. Listen to regulate.

item.title: Why a Wrong Explanation Can Feel So Right
item.description:
Cognition

Why a Wrong Explanation Can Feel So Right

Our need to resolve uncertainty can shape what we believe.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • An “aha” moment can make an accompanying belief seem more truthful.
  • The desire for certainty can make us less receptive to alternative explanations.
  • Uncertainty can intensify both unpleasant and pleasant emotional experiences.
  • An explanation can provide psychological value without providing evidence that it is true.

What I love about psychology is how it presents itself in the everyday experiences we all have. Here’s a little example from me this week that got me thinking about the relationship between feeling and knowing.

As coffee lovers, my partner and I recently purchased a new coffee machine with two independent elements: a filter with a hot plate, and a pod dispenser. Last week, I made a travel-mug quantity of coffee into the jug. My partner then prepared her usual latte using the pod dispenser. When I returned for a second cup, I noticed the hot plate was off. I instantly assumed that using the pod side must switch off the hot plate. This happened again, which strengthened my confidence sufficiently that I told my partner that this was how the machine worked and that she needed to switch the hot plate back on.

The following day, I noticed that preparing a quantity of coffee sufficient for a travel mug didn’t activate the hot plate. So it wasn’t that the two parts of the machine were autonomous; rather, the key variable was the quantity of coffee selected: travel mug quantities don’t activate the hot plate.

My plausible explanation had mutated to established fact before it had even been tested. I had inferred a causal relationship without sufficient actual evidence to support this idea.

When the Stakes Are Higher

This got me thinking about how often we make an observation, infer some meaning or cause, seek confirmation, then develop a degree of confidence in our assumption and communicate this idea to someone else, solidifying it even more.

While this is of little consequence for my coffee machine experience, when we consider examples in life that are more emotionally provoking and relate to health, work, relationships, and our sense of identity, the stakes are somewhat higher.

As I thought about this a little more, it seemed apparent that we frequently assign an immediate explanation to experiences. A difficult relationship could be seen as an attachment problem. Someone behaving in a selfish way can be deemed a narcissist. Fatigue or exhaustion might be seen as evidence of nervous system dysregulation, or difficulty concentrating could be interpreted as ADHD.

Of course, some of these explanations may be true. But that’s not the point I’m making. The more interesting psychological question for me was: Why does an explanation that feels so plausible so easily become an explanation that feels absolute and true?

The question I kept coming back to was: What is this explanation doing beyond simply providing information?

There is some interesting research that might help us understand this. In a series of experiments by cognitive scientist Ruben Laukkonen and colleagues, people were presented with statements about the world while having to solve an anagram connected to completing the sentence. Sometimes solving the anagram produced an “aha” experience internally, the feeling that something has just clicked into place.

But the really interesting part was that the insight derived from solving the anagram provided no evidence that the statement they were reading was actually true. Yet, when people experienced that “aha” moment, they rated the completed statement as more truthful.

This is termed “insight misattribution”: the positive feeling accompanying an insight or discovery that spills over and influences some other belief or statement.

This is not to say that the feeling is always wrong because sometimes it will be right. But we need to be careful, because the feeling that something has clicked into place does not necessarily tell us that what has clicked into place is factually correct.

Why Do We Want To Know?

Sometimes we aren't simply trying to find the right explanation. We're also trying to stop not knowing.

Psychologists Arie Kruglanski and Donna Webster have described this as a need for “cognitive closure.” This essentially means that we have a desire for a definite answer to diminish our uncertainty or ambiguity. Their research suggests something particularly interesting can happen when this need becomes stronger. We can “seize” on an explanation relatively quickly and then “freeze” on it, becoming less receptive to alternative possibilities.

There are very good reasons the mind behaves in this way. Life is full of incomplete explanations, yet action is frequently required. We tend to infer, predict, and fill in the gaps, and most of the time this works well. Attempting to implement a scientific approach to every decision we make would be functionally impossible.

The challenge arises when the line blurs between what we observed and what we inferred, particularly when the explanation concerns something of importance.

But I think there's another layer worth exploring. Uncertainty is more than just an intellectual experience; it brings an emotional charge. In a series of experiments, Yoav Bar-Anan and colleagues investigated whether simply feeling uncertain could influence related emotional responses. They found that uncertainty intensified reactions to both unpleasant and pleasant experiences.

Imagine you receive a text from your partner saying, “Can we talk tonight?” The uncertainty will likely generate some internal feelings, and you might find yourself revisiting thoughts in an attempt to uncover a plausible explanation. If, on the other hand, the text reads, “Can we talk tonight about where we go for dinner on Friday?” there is no uncertainty and less emotional charge.

Another example could be receiving a text that says, “I’ve got a surprise for you tonight.” This uncertainty might trigger anticipation and some pleasant emotions. If a second text reveals the nature of the surprise, the pleasant anticipatory emotions may be diminished. That’s why we might say, “Don’t tell me, you’ll spoil the surprise.” Our motivation to resolve uncertainty could depend on the emotional experience that accompanies it.

From a mind-body perspective, I sometimes think of repetitive thinking as an attempt to resolve an uncomfortable state of uncertainty. Additional information or an explanation may close the loop.

Uncertainty that feels threatening can motivate us towards an explanation that closes the loop. But closing that loop doesn’t always end discomfort. There are instances where the explanation gives rise to more negative feelings.

When uncertainty feels threatening, the drive to find an explanation may partly become a drive to change the experience of not knowing. Closure doesn’t necessarily make us feel better, but it does give us something more concrete to feel bad about.

There is an important distinction between how an explanation serves us and what the evidence actually tells us. An explanation can make sense of an uncertain experience, give it meaning and predictability, which in turn could give closure. While these are of great psychological value, they don’t necessarily provide evidence that the explanation itself is true.

Separating Observation From Interpretation

There's an irony here that we should consider. I've just spent the last few minutes offering you an explanation for why explanations can feel convincing. And if something in this post has produced its own little “aha,” then my argument suggests you shouldn't accept it simply because it feels right either.

The useful thing about my coffee-machine explanation wasn't eventually finding another explanation that felt more convincing. It was discovering a way to test which explanation was actually right. My experience taught me that posing some questions can help prevent becoming attached to an observation too quickly. You can ask yourself:

  1. What did I directly observe?
  2. What feelings are present in my body?
  3. What have I inferred from my observation?
  4. Which other explanations remain possible?
  5. What evidence would cause me to revise my conclusions?
  6. What does having an explanation do for me?

Bringing some scientific thinking into our everyday lives is not the absence of assumptions; rather, it’s the discipline of making those assumptions more visible so we can test them before they turn into “facts.”

The feeling that something makes sense is a reason to investigate an explanation. It isn't evidence enough to stop investigating.
